opus-5.5.text:
Right now, the way I use these models is mostly transactional. I ask a question, get an answer, maybe iterate a few times, and then the context is gone. What I'd really like is something closer to a colleague who's been working alongside me for months. It would know what I'm trying to do, what I've already tried, what my taste is, and where I tend to go wrong.

Concretely, a few things come to mind.

**Longer horizons.** Instead of helping with a single function or paragraph, I'd want to hand off a whole chunk of a project, like "go investigate why this training run is unstable." It would come back a few hours later having run the experiments, read the logs, ruled some hypotheses out, and written up what it found. That's the shift from a tool you query to a collaborator you delegate to.

**Proactivity, with judgment.** A good collaborator doesn't just answer what you asked. They say, "I think you're asking the wrong question," or "this result looks suspicious, have you checked the eval?" I'd like models that push back when it's warranted, but that also know when to stay out of the way. Calibrating that is tricky.

**Knowing what it doesn't know.** For research especially, the most valuable thing is often an honest assessment of uncertainty. If it's confident, say so. If it's guessing, I want to know. Overconfident collaborators are worse than useless, because you end up redoing their work.

**Shared context and memory.** It should be able to read the codebase, my notes, and past discussions. So much friction comes from re-explaining things. If it carried that state forward, the collaboration would compound over time instead of resetting every session.

The part I find most interesting is the transition. At first you check everything it does. Gradually you build trust in certain domains and stop checking as closely, the same way you would with a new person on your team. I think getting that trust-building process right, so it's earned and well-founded rather than blind, is one of the more important problems, both for usefulness and for safety.

r001.rationale: It describes a collaborator that knows what the user is trying to do and has already tried, and carries shared project context forward over time.

r002.rationale: It says the collaborator should proactively flag issues and suggest checks, such as asking whether the user has checked the eval.

r003.rationale: It proposes handing off a project chunk and having the collaborator investigate in the background, then report back hours later with findings.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I'd most like to see is for the assistant to move from being something you query to something that's actually keeping track of your work over time. Right now the interaction is still pretty stateless. You open a session, you explain the context, you get some help, and then it all evaporates. What I want is more like a colleague who's been in the room for the last six months. They know which experiments we ran, which ideas got abandoned and why, what my half-formed hunches are. So when I come back and say "let's try that thing again," they know what I mean.

The other piece is proactivity, but done carefully. I don't want something constantly interrupting me, but I do want it to notice things. If I'm writing an analysis and it's quietly aware that the dataset I'm using has a known issue, or that someone on the team already tried this approach last month, it should bring that up. The best human collaborators do that. They connect dots you didn't ask them to connect.

And then there's the longer-horizon stuff. I'd love to be able to hand off a genuinely open-ended research question, something that's going to take days of iteration, and have the assistant go run experiments, hit dead ends, come back with "here's what I tried, here's what surprised me, here's where I'm stuck." That requires a kind of taste and judgment about what's worth pursuing that models are only starting to develop. They're good at executing a well-specified task. They're less good at knowing when the task itself was the wrong one.

I think the honest state of things is that the models are already pretty strong at the raw capability, and a lot of what's missing is on the systems side. Memory, tooling, the ability to act in the world and get feedback. So I expect the next couple of years to feel less like the models getting smarter in the abstract and more like them becoming actually embedded in how work gets done. That's the shift I'm most excited about.

r001.rationale: The response describes an assistant that retains project context over time, including experiments, abandoned ideas and their reasons, and the user’s hunches.

r002.rationale: It says the assistant should proactively notice and bring up relevant information, but does not clearly propose suggesting things for the user to try.

r003.rationale: It proposes handing off an open-ended research question for the assistant to run experiments on and report back about.

astra-6.text:
I’d like them to be able to take on longer pieces of work without needing me to specify every step. Right now, a lot of the interaction is: I ask a question, get an answer, and then figure out what to ask next. I’d like the assistant to share more of that responsibility—to keep track of what we’re trying to accomplish, notice when an approach isn’t working, and suggest what to try next.

For research, that might mean going from a vague idea to an experiment, looking at the results, and helping decide whether the idea is worth pursuing. The important thing is that it stays easy to understand and steer. I want it to exercise judgment about when to work independently and when there’s a consequential choice where we should talk.

r001.rationale: The response says the assistant should track what they are trying to accomplish, but does not say it maintains context of everything the user has done on the project.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the assistant should suggest what to try next when an approach is not working.

r003.rationale: It describes longer work and independent judgment, but does not say the assistant works on the project in the background.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like them to take on more of the work of figuring out how to help. Right now, you often have to formulate a pretty precise question, give them the relevant context, and then check the answer. That’s useful, but it still leaves a lot of the burden on you.

For research, I’d want an assistant that can follow a line of inquiry with me over time. It would understand what we’re trying to figure out, suggest an experiment, help run it, and then look at the results and say, “Actually, this doesn’t distinguish between these two explanations.” And it should be willing to push back when an idea doesn’t make sense.

The tricky part is getting the right balance of initiative and oversight. I don’t want to approve every little step, but I do want it to surface assumptions and ask when there’s an important decision. Ideally, delegating something would feel like handing it to a thoughtful colleague: you can leave it with them, and they come back with useful progress and a clear account of what they’re uncertain about.

r001.rationale: It says the assistant should follow a line of inquiry over time, but does not clearly say it will retain context of everything the user has done on the project.

r002.rationale: It proposes that the assistant suggest an experiment for the user to try.

r003.rationale: It describes delegating work, leaving it with the assistant, and returning later to useful progress, which communicates background project work.
